extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy of science, logic of induction, and scientific method; scientists interested in evaluating evidence and hypotheses
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for judging testimony, anomalies, coincidences, miracles, and scientific hypotheses according to the logic of induction — when to believe, suspend judgment, or reject claims and when hypotheses are legitimate. Applies to assessment of empirical claims and formulation/verification of hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Law rejection requires equivalent evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: A law received on what seemed a complete induction can only be rejected on evidence equivalent; the law can be rejected only by evidence inconsistent with it and consistent with some other and better established law of nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an alleged fact appears to contradict a law of nature established by induction, one must either disbelieve the alleged fact or abandon the law — and abandoning the law requires evidence at least as strong as that on which the law was originally established. A genuine conflict between two supposed laws must end in the total rejection of one, because there must be a flaw in the logical process by which one or the other was established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Miracle understood as introduction of a new cause
rubrics_metrics.description: A miracle is not a contradiction to the law of cause and effect but a new effect supposed to be produced by the introduction of a new cause.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a cause adequate to produce the supposed miracle were present, its adequacy is not in doubt; hence the only antecedent improbability ascribed to a miracle is the improbability that any such cause existed. Therefore, testimony for a miracle can only persuade those who already admit the possibility of supernatural agents, or where the evidence makes the supernatural cause more probable than unknown natural causes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Always consider unknown natural-cause hypothesis
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a marvelous fact is well attested, there remains the hypothesis that it was due to some unknown natural cause rather than supernatural intervention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No amount of ordinary certification can prove an event to be a miracle unless the possibility of some unknown natural agency can be completely excluded; thus, when evaluating miraculous claims, weigh the plausibility of unknown natural explanations before inferring supernatural agency.

rubrics_metrics.name: Presumption against special divine interpositions
rubrics_metrics.description: Because the government of the universe is generally carried on by general laws, there is a general presumption against supposing divine agency not operating through general laws.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This antecedent improbability in every alleged miracle requires extraordinary antecedent probability from the special circumstances of the case in order to outweigh it; judges should weigh conformity of the result to the supposed agent's character (e.g., the deity's character) as part of this assessment.

rubrics_metrics.name: To contradict a causal law, absence of adequate counteracting cause must be shown
rubrics_metrics.description: An allegation that a cause existed without the expected effect must show that this happened in the absence of any adequate counteracting cause; otherwise it is not a contradiction to the causal law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing evidence that seems to violate a causal law, estimate whether any known or unknown counteracting causes likely existed at the specific time and place — use prior knowledge of the frequency or rarity of such causes to judge antecedent improbability of their presence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Estimate counteracting-cause probability from prior frequency at time/place
rubrics_metrics.description: For known causes capable of counteracting a given cause, use previous knowledge of their frequency or rarity to infer the antecedent improbability of their having been present in the particular case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: We are required only to judge the probability of such causes having existed at the time and place alleged, not their general existence in nature. Consider whether such causes would have manifested by other marks, or whether an unknown cause would have hitherto manifested elsewhere.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish conflicts with laws of causation vs uniformities of coexistence (Kinds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Alleged facts may conflict either with completely ascertained causal laws or with mere uniformities of coexistence (properties of Kinds); these should be treated differently in evaluation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Facts contradicting causal laws require far stronger grounds for belief or otherwise must be rejected unless they point to another law. Facts that would establish a new Kind are not inherently impossible and should be rejected only if the improbability (e.g., that such a variety should have been undiscovered) exceeds the probability of error or mendacity in witnesses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suspend judgment for anomalies that do not violate most general laws
rubrics_metrics.description: When an alleged fact conflicts only with limited or special generalizations (not near-universal laws), it is often wise to suspend judgment and await confirmation from subsequent observers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In cases like reports from unexplored regions or rare natural variants (e.g., flying fish, ornithorhynchus), if credible witnesses report a novel Kind, regard the report as requiring confirmation rather than immediate rejection, unless the alleged properties conflict with more comprehensive generalizations that approach causal laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to absolutely general laws are permanently incredible
rubrics_metrics.description: Uniformities true of all things (e.g., laws of number and extension, and perhaps the law of causation itself) approach such generality that an exception to them is absolutely and permanently incredible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only assertions contradicting these most general laws are typically labeled 'impossible' (total impossibility). Violations of less-general laws should be called impossible only 'in the circumstances of the case' and otherwise treated as improbable rather than absolutely incredible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sift testimony for suspicious circumstances and common causes of false testimony
rubrics_metrics.description: Testimony that survives careful sifting is rare; untrustworthy testimony is usually associated with fallacious appearances, epidemic delusions, or strong interests (religious zeal, party feeling, vanity, passion for the marvellous).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing testimony for extraordinary claims, look for signs that could account for the witnesses' impressions (optical illusions, delusions, social contagion) or motives that might bias them. If such circumstances are present and more probable than the alleged fact, disbelieve the testimony; otherwise weigh conviction proportionally and consider further investigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Differentiate improbability before the fact vs after the fact
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a crucial distinction between improbability before an event (the improbability of a guess) and improbability after being informed that an event occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: An event being unlikely a priori (e.g., one face of a die) is not a reason to disbelieve credible testimony that it occurred, because some particular unlikely outcome must occur. Thus unusualness alone does not justify disbelief; evaluate according to whether the event is contrary to any induction or general law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Coincidences often require additional scrutiny
rubrics_metrics.description: Coincidences — peculiar, unexpected regularities — are often regarded as more improbable and thought to require stronger evidence than ordinary events.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Part of this impression derives from the rarity of personal experience of such coincidences and from motives to falsehood (the desire to astonish). When evaluating a claimed coincidence, estimate whether the testimony is more likely to have been produced falsely (motivations, misperception) than the coincidence having actually occurred; however, assessment must be made from first principles in each instance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compare causes: design vs chance for remarkable regularities
rubrics_metrics.description: When a very regular or striking series occurs (e.g., repeated sixes), we should consider whether it is more likely due to chance or to a constant/design cause (e.g., unfair dice).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Attribute an observed regularity to the cause that would more readily produce it. The superior efficacy of a constant cause (design) will quickly outweigh any antecedent improbability of that cause's existence; weigh comparative probabilities of chance vs design.

rubrics_metrics.name: Laplace-style base-rate reasoning for testimony of rare outcomes (and its limits)
rubrics_metrics.description: Laplace argues that testimony of a very rare outcome (white ball among 999 black) is less credible because false announcements will disproportionately produce the rare report; thus rare events need stronger testimony.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Apply base-rate thinking: if a witness has a certain error/fraud rate, false reports will affect rare outcomes disproportionately. But be cautious: the argument assumes the witness's pattern of error is uniform across alternatives; in many real cases this assumption fails (different forms of error or motives may change error distribution). Therefore assess whether the witness's error tendencies make Laplace's reasoning applicable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate whether testimony would plausibly be asserted if the fact were false
rubrics_metrics.description: To decide credibility of testimony for an unusual claim, estimate the probability that the given testimony would have been delivered in that instance, supposing the fact asserted were not true.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This first-principles approach requires considering the witness's likely errors, biases, motives, and the space of possible false assertions — do not rely on blanket rules; analyze the particular context to judge how likely false testimony is relative to true testimony.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legitimacy of scientific hypotheses: rules of hypothesis vs rules of induction
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses are not held to the same standard as inductive proof; it is legitimate to propose hypotheses that are not yet proved, provided they meet the rules of hypothesis (testability, deducible consequences).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A hypothesis is legitimate if one can deduce consequences and compare them with facts such that the hypothesis can be disproved if ill-founded. The text cites Broussais, Gilbert, and Darwin as examples where bold hypotheses were justified because they were testable and useful for guiding inquiry, even if initial grounds were slight.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vera causa criterion for explanatory hypotheses
rubrics_metrics.description: An explanatory hypothesis should, where possible, be a 'vera causa' — a true cause — or at least be shown capable of producing effects of the same kind as those attributed to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The hypothesis of natural selection is lauded as not only a vera causa but 'one proved to be capable of producing effects of the same kind with those which the hypothesis ascribes to it.' Use evidence that the proposed cause can produce comparable effects when judging legitimacy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Tentative hypotheses can be justified to stimulate inquiry despite weak initial grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: It is sometimes proper to frame tentative hypotheses on slight grounds to open paths of inquiry, even though verification may be difficult and the original grounds inadequate for proof.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propose tentative hypotheses when they can be used to deduce consequences and guide investigation (e.g., Gall's phrenology or speculative ideas about brain electricity). Yet remain cautious: verification difficulties or methodological incompetence may render some tentatively proposed hypotheses premature or misleading.
